| Public notice | Users receive a verified condition statement | Current notice/history route |
| Quiet visit | Contact occurs only in agreed conditions | Quest/relationship owner |
| Deferred obligation | A later review is required before use | Project/history owner if approved |

The agreement exists only if its current authority can retain and expose it. A dialogue option alone cannot create a persistent rule.

### Field 03 expansion — small agreement and notice records

| Candidate record | Required source | Player choice | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| agree_pump_draw_window | Water owner result | Accept, amend, or defer | Current allocation state |
| agree_bridge_load_limit | Inspection receipt | Post, re-inspect, or close | Route limitation |
| agree_relay_open_hours | Custodian plus service state | Shared or limited access | Communications/access result |
| agree_store_entry | Food/site inspection | Allow, restrict, or move stock | Site and food state |
| agree_room_use | Receiving-site inspection | Prepare, restrict, or cancel | Room readiness |
| notice_work_paused | Actual pause reason | Publish or keep internal | Notice owner result |
| notice_inspection_rejected | Service-owner rejection | Correct or appeal | Updated public state |
| notice_no_fault_found | Completed inspection | Close or seek more evidence | No repair mutation |
| notice_delivery_changed | Inventory/route receipt | Reroute or wait | Delivery result |
| notice_access_disputed | Conflicting authorization | Request review or defer | Dispute retained |
| notice_followup_due | Existing result receipt | Schedule or dismiss | Callback eligibility |
| notice_service_restricted | Current owner restriction | Explain terms | Restricted state visible |

These records provide a concrete data review list without creating a notice authority alongside existing UI/history owners.

### Field 04 expansion — character continuity rules

Characters remember only a few observable facts: whether the player asked before entering; whether a promised notice was delivered; whether the stated limit was followed; whether an inspection was requested; and whether a request was left open. Each memory links to a current quest result. Character dialogue does not infer secret motives or change an independent relationship meter.

If a person moves or becomes unavailable through current campaign systems, later content uses the canonical availability result. A story can replace a planned meeting with a written note only when the current quest system supports that fallback. This preserves continuity across different campaign states.

### Field 05 expansion — agreement and access task lot

| Task | Player action | Result |
|---|---|---|
| confirm_witnessed_limit | Ask two affected users to inspect the notice | Notice has two sources |
| request_shift_exception | Contact access owner | Window approved or denied |
| reconcile_key_custody | Compare item and access receipts | Current holder verified or unknown |
| explain_pause_reason | Return to the proposer | Request acknowledged or still disputed |
| amend_shared_hours | Gather availability from two groups | New schedule is owner-approved or pending |
| mark_temporary_load | Post an accepted route rule | Map shows actual restriction |
| retrieve_old_notice | Compare previous and current condition | Revision history retained |
| ask_for_reinspection | Submit new evidence | Inspector scheduled or unavailable |
| close_unused_delivery | Cancel a reserved shipment | Inventory/route results reconciled |
| return_after_first_use | Inspect the service after opening | Owner result refreshed |
| identify_public_contact | Find an authorized spokesperson | Contact information verified |
| correct_wrong_site_name | Confirm the alias with a local witness | Map owner accepts correction |

### Field 06 expansion — agreements across existing owners

The project coordinator, if one is ever approved, should store references to service agreements rather than reproduce their state. An access condition belongs to the location owner; an item loan belongs to inventory; a route limit belongs to travel/map; a staff schedule belongs to duty; and a receiving-site condition belongs to the room or medical owner. The coordinator can display the combined agreement summary only when all references are current.

If one agreement spans several owners, acceptance is staged. The player sees which sub-operation failed and whether accepted sub-operations rolled back. The plan does not assume that an agreement is atomic across owners without an existing transaction contract.

### Field 07 expansion — agreement review route

The proposed agreement view has four tabs: terms, evidence, affected services, and history. Terms show current scope and duration or state that duration is unknown. Evidence shows the source and date. Affected services link to their owners. History lists accepted revisions. The screen is read-only until a valid owner command is available.

Before changing a term, show its current value and the proposed replacement. The player can back out without modifying the current agreement. A stale agreement is labelled stale and can be rechecked through its owner rather than silently updated.

### Field 08 expansion — disputes and correction

When residents disagree with a technical limit, keep the technical result and the social disagreement separate. The player can gather another inspection, explain the limit, request an owner review, or leave the dispute open. Do not change a route or service state because the UI records a complaint.

Correction notices link the old source to the new result and identify what changed. The correction should be short enough to read in a worksite context and detailed enough to explain the permitted action. Accessible text labels accompany map symbols and status colors.

### Field 09 expansion — agreement history workload

Profile 6, 24, and 60 agreement references; 10 active projects; 100 sites; and 200 historical closeouts. Measure the agreement view without loading every closed project’s full detail. Test that revision changes update all projections and that stale references produce a clear refresh request rather than a null display.

### Field 10 expansion — package acceptance

One agreement package is ready when it demonstrates a supported rule, current owner command, named evidence, visible terms, failure/rollback behavior, save ownership, and a later review. It must also show an honest no-agreement route. The first two agreement types should use different current owners to prove that the display does not become a hidden authority.

If the current game already exposes the needed agreement and history routes, treat these cards as content improvements and route them to their owner. Create no new shared agreement store until the foreman confirms an evidence-backed gap and assigns the exact implementation package.

## Pass 9 — Community use cases and decision-ready project cards

### Field 01 expansion — the public result after first use

The first use of a repaired service is a playable moment, not an automatic victory screen. A player can return with a user, observe whether the service is accessible under its posted terms, and ask the relevant owner for its current state. The user may report a problem that the service owner has not yet confirmed. The player can log the report, request another inspection, or close it as unverified. This makes follow-up useful without immediately reopening completed work.

### Field 02 expansion — accepted-result language

Every project closes with one of four labels: accepted service; accepted restriction; work reported but awaiting confirmation; or closed without a service change. The label comes from the current owner receipt. A character’s gratitude, anger, or relief can accompany the result but cannot substitute for it. If an owner returns no result, the project remains pending or closes as incomplete according to its contract.

### Field 03 expansion — result card examples

| Result card | Player-facing text | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| Pump limited | The water owner confirms limited draw under the posted schedule | Recheck after agreed period |
| Crossing restricted | The route owner reports a load limit remains active | Request a new inspection |
| Relay unverified | Work was reported, but communications service was not confirmed | Run an owner-supported signal check |
| Room ready | The site owner confirms the room can receive the planned visit | Schedule through current owner |
| Stock held | The food owner has not cleared the affected lot | Find alternate stock or wait |
| No fault found | Inspection did not confirm the original report | Close the proposal without consuming repair goods |

### Field 04 expansion — local use scenes

Add brief scenes where an actual user attempts the changed service: a cart approaches the limited crossing; a household asks when the pump is available; a courier checks whether the relay accepts a message; a caregiver inspects the receiving room; or a storekeeper seeks the latest stock disposition. Each scene uses the current owner result and offers a distinct response if the user’s need falls outside the accepted conditions.

### Field 05 expansion — short return quests

| Quest | Trigger | Action |
|---|---|---|
| inspect_first_use | Owner reports a reopened service | Visit with a valid user |
| clarify_posted_hours | User cannot read the schedule | Correct the approved notice |
| request_second_limit | New evidence challenges a restriction | Ask the route/service owner |
| find_alternate_service | Project remains deferred | Check a known alternate |
| close_no_fault | Inspection found no defect | Tell requester and close |
| report_new_damage | New source describes a change | Open a fresh proposal |
| reconcile_returned_part | Work canceled after reservation | Confirm inventory receipt |
| review_shared_window | Agreement review time arrives | Confirm or request amendment |

### Field 06 expansion — existing plan handoff boundary

Return scenes may reveal gaps in construction, communications, access, or project history. They do not authorize changes to those owners. A handoff names the accepted plan, evidence, missing consumer or result, and exact owner. If a current unblocked plan can use the scene or project card, transfer it through the integration process instead of creating a competing public-works package.

### Field 07 expansion — result navigation

From a result card, the player can open the owner’s current service page, review the original proposal, read the public notice, or accept a supported follow-up. The result screen remains read-only after closeout. New work begins through the owning system or a new proposal command, never by reopening the old receipt and mutating history.

### Field 08 expansion — accessibility and conflict copy

Use text labels for acceptance, restriction, pending confirmation, and no change. Explain disputes with their sources and consequences. Do not use red/green alone to distinguish a failed inspection from an accepted restriction. The player can navigate the result and its evidence with keyboard or controller and return to the previous site.

### Field 09 expansion — historical and live-state split

Measure a campaign with 200 closed results and 10 active projects. Opening history loads a compact summary; opening one result fetches its details. The current service view always reads the owner. If the current state has changed since the project closed, show the old accepted result beside the present state instead of replacing it.

### Field 10 expansion — final card review

Before a project card enters the first playable tranche, confirm a real user action, an owner result, one honest no-change branch, one follow-up, complete public language, and an evidence trail. Reject cards that only increase a generic community score or repeat a completed construction/colony workflow without adding a distinct regional service interaction.

## Pass 10 — Worksite continuity and public-use verification

### Field 01 expansion — player return loop

After a project closes, the player can return to the site when a new source or scheduled review makes the visit relevant. The visit reveals current owner truth, a user’s practical experience, or a changed condition. It does not reopen the old project automatically.

### Field 02 expansion — new evidence rule

New damage, a missed agreement, or a changed service is a new report linked to the previous result. The player can compare the history and current owner state before deciding to open another task. No narrative line directly changes completed project state.

### Field 03 expansion — return visit cards

| Card | Trigger | Result |
|---|---|---|
| first_pump_draw | Water owner confirms limited service | Confirm or report a new issue |
| bridge_notice_review | New user reports confusion | Correct or retain the posted rule |
| relay_first_message | Communications owner confirms service | Review delivery and access |
| room_first_visit | Receiving site becomes active | Confirm readiness through its owner |
| store_disposition | Food owner resolves a hold | Review stock result |

### Field 04 expansion — aftermath writing

Aftermath scenes use three facts: what the player promised, what the owner confirmed, and what the local user experienced. A character may still disagree. This keeps story closure human while leaving state truth explicit.

### Field 05 expansion — return objectives

The return quest can ask the player to verify a notice, retrieve a tool, close a debt, request another inspection, or record a new access problem. Every task can be declined and remains tied to an existing owner result.

### Field 06 expansion — history ownership

Historical project outcomes should use the current chronicle, journal, or project owner. A new task references the old receipt and stores only its own new result. Do not create a duplicate lifetime work ledger.

### Field 07 expansion — site panel

The site panel separates current service, last project result, new reports, and available commands. It identifies dates and sources and returns the player to the same map selection after closing a detail view.

### Field 08 expansion — readable changes

Show the difference between “project accepted,” “service available,” and “user confirms first use.” Use text labels, not just marker color. A disputed report can coexist with a confirmed older result.

### Field 09 expansion — campaign history

Review long campaigns with several completed projects and changed services. Confirm that old result links remain valid, new inspections do not duplicate completed callbacks, and the active site view does not display stale project data as current.

### Field 10 expansion — verification boundary

The worksite handoff lists the last accepted receipt, current owner query, new report, save behavior, visible site card, and closeout rule. If an owner cannot report first use, the narrative may describe a witnessed visit but cannot claim a general service guarantee.

## Pass 11 — Public works package catalogue, inspection receipts, and neighborhood arcs

This pass adds a work-order workbook and civic story material to the existing ten-field structure. It does not create a second construction system, civic currency, labor pool, materials ledger, site graph, or contract authority. The project records below are proposals for content and integration review. A work order becomes playable only when the current site, inventory, duty, construction, travel, and persistence owners can support its concrete command and result.

### Field 01 expansion — public works as a sequence of commitments

A public project is a public promise. The player should see who requested it, who will be affected, what evidence supports the request, which authority owns the work, how long the commitment remains open, and what can still change. The project lifecycle distinguishes proposal, inspection, scoped work, accepted schedule, active work, inspection result, handoff, and maintenance follow-up. Those words are a planning vocabulary; reuse current state where it exists instead of adding another project state machine.

The player’s choice may determine priority or consent to a public disruption, but a choice should not manufacture labor, material, construction progress, or ownership. When the canonical owner refuses a project because an input is unavailable, the work order remains visible with that reason. If the current implementation cannot express a particular commitment, keep the scope as a draft and do not simulate completion in prose.

Projects should be legible to residents who disagree. An inspection can confirm that a defect exists without proving which group is responsible. A work plan can benefit one route and inconvenience another. A “complete” label should mean the owning system completed the work, and should state which parts were inspected. Maintenance obligations remain visible after construction so that a one-time upgrade is not mistaken for permanent service.

### Field 02 expansion — work packet and closeout contract

A candidate work packet contains: work ID, title, requester, affected locations, source evidence, current site owner, scope, exclusions, materials quote source, labor quote source, access needs, accepted start condition, progress receipt, inspection owner, closeout receipt, maintenance owner, and unresolved objection. These fields are documentation prompts, not an approved serialized schema.

A receipt should name the outcome rather than only mark a checkbox. Examples: inspection completed; site unavailable; scope revised; materials not reserved; work began; work stopped; repair accepted; repair rejected with evidence; follow-up due; or unresolved access dispute. Receipts should identify their source and timestamp or simulation step. Never encode civic approval solely as dialogue text if later screens need to know it.

The closeout record should include what was done, what was not done, who accepted it, what remains disputed, and how to reopen maintenance through the current owner. If the work changes an existing site, call that owner; do not mirror site state inside the public works catalog. Historical records should be append-only if the current journal or work log has that contract, preserving why a scope changed.

### Field 03 expansion — candidate project catalogue

| Working project | Request and inspection focus | Scope boundary | Closeout question |
|---|---|---|---|
| North Lane Drain | Residents report standing water near a shared lane | Inspect existing drainage and submit an owner-supported repair if available | Did the repair owner verify the flow condition afterward? |
| Winter Notice Board | Several groups receive different versions of a closure notice | Replace or correct the notice using an existing interaction | Which revision is current, and where is the old one archived? |
| Market Awning Frame | Stall holders request shade after repeated fabric failure | Inspect supports and record a repair plan without inventing a weather mechanic | Who accepted the repaired frame and maintenance duty? |
| Clinic Footpath | Visitors describe a difficult approach to an existing service site | Review access using current map/site owners and request a supported path change | Is accessibility confirmed by the responsible site owner? |
| Shared Tool Locker | Work crews disagree about missing tool custody | Establish check-in and return receipts through existing inventory conventions | Are custody records distinct from stock mutation? |
| Lower Steps Rail | Residents report a damaged handrail at a public stair | Inspect, scope repair, and communicate temporary access status | Which system controls stair/site availability? |
| School Roof Tarp | A temporary covering is repeatedly displaced | Record inspection findings, repair or relocate meeting through supported site actions | Did the building become usable, or only receive a temporary cover? |
| Pump Yard Sign | Crews cannot tell which valve notice is current | Update an instruction card after owner review | Was the revised text approved by the current service owner? |
| Seed Store Ramp | A hand cart cannot reach the storage threshold easily | Inspect the existing entrance and propose an access improvement | Who verifies access and what route does the cart use? |
| East Fence Gate | Neighbors disagree about who may pass through a shared gate | Facilitate a documented access agreement before construction | Was agreement voluntary and is dissent retained? |
| Ash Lane Marker | Old and new route markings conflict | Audit source dates and replace only the superseded marker | Does the map owner agree with the marker placement? |
| Workshop Vent Cover | Repair crew reports a loose cover and uncertain work boundary | Inspect and assign the maintenance owner | Is the finding limited to the observed panel? |
| Meeting Hall Benches | A gathering place lacks seating for a planned meeting | Reuse or produce items only through current construction/inventory paths | Were the benches transferred and accepted? |
| Waste Sorting Shelter | Residents request separate storage areas | Test whether current waste authority supports category separation | If unsupported, is the proposal clearly deferred? |
| River Steps Landing | Boat users ask for a visible wait point | Review access and sign placement without promising boat service | Is the landing open according to the route owner? |
| Quiet Hours Notice | Nearby residents request a shared notice about work hours | Record a public agreement and a dissent channel | Can the agreement be revised without erasing its history? |
| Lantern Repair Bench | A well-used public lamp station has no repair surface | Connect a maintenance request to an existing workshop/site seam | Does the site owner expose the actual new interaction? |
| Upper Store Roof | A leak report conflicts with a prior repair receipt | Reinspect and preserve both observations until resolved | Does the new result supersede the old claim with evidence? |

These projects are intentionally varied across access, maintenance, communication, custody, and public agreement. They should not all become one generic construction mission. Each one needs a distinct owner, practical consequence, and player-visible closure.

### Field 04 expansion — neighborhood story arcs

**The lane that serves two blocks.** A drainage repair is requested by residents on both sides of a narrow lane. One group wants immediate access restored; the other worries that a repair will direct runoff toward their doorway. The player first gathers separate observations, then requests an inspection. If the owner can model a repair, the player can choose among supported scopes. If it cannot, the story can close with a temporary notice and a documented unresolved concern. The story does not reward the player for ignoring a minority report.

**The tool ledger.** Three crews share one tool locker. A missing item is blamed on the latest crew, but check-in records are incomplete. The player can ask each custodian for a statement, compare existing inventory evidence, and introduce a handoff receipt if an approved inventory interaction supports it. One branch recovers the item; another finds that it was moved to a site with no return note. Both endings improve clarity without labeling a character dishonest without evidence.

**A meeting with no accessible entrance.** A public meeting is scheduled at a hall whose entrance has a known barrier. The player may select another supported site, postpone the meeting, or pursue a verified access repair. Attendees can disagree about delay. The story presents who was unable to attend and what choice was made, rather than treating attendance count as a sufficient outcome. Any accessibility work must route through current site and UI owners; no local “accessible” flag can override actual reachability.

**The notice that outlived the repair.** A warning sign remains after the repair owner has issued a completion receipt. Some residents trust the old sign because it prevented an accident. The player compares the dated source and proposes a replacement that preserves the reason for caution. The closeout removes stale public instructions only when the owner confirms the route or facility state. The old text remains in history to explain the change.

### Field 05 expansion — public task and side-quest workbook

Candidate tasks, each with a single completion receipt:

- Photograph or transcribe the source of a drainage complaint.
- Ask both affected blocks for separate access observations.
- Request a site inspection through the current owner.
- Publish a temporary closure notice using supported map/site state.
- Reconcile a tool handoff with canonical inventory.
- Return an item to its recorded custodian.
- Compare an old notice with the current owner receipt.
- Find a meeting place that the current site catalog exposes.
- Ask a resident to review the wording of a public notice.
- Record a resident’s objection without blocking unrelated work.
- Deliver an accepted material quote to the work planner.
- Check whether labor availability still matches the agreed schedule.
- Confirm a work crew’s arrival through the current travel path.
- Inspect a repaired gate with both neighbor representatives present.
- Separate “work complete” from “inspection accepted.”
- Schedule maintenance only if an owner exposes a real maintenance command.
- Reopen an issue after a newer contradictory report.
- Explain a project refusal using its actual failed precondition.
- Retire a superseded notice while preserving the prior version.
- Close a project with a named remaining obligation.
- Transfer responsibility to the next shift with a receipt.
- Publish an interim agreement with review date and dissent reference.
- Revisit a public work site after a simulated time step only if the owner supports it.
- Compare the work order against the current map before claiming route access.

An optional objective should add a meaningful point of view or follow-up, not require repetitive delivery of materials. A side quest can resolve through a careful handoff, clear refusal, or acknowledgement of missing authority. Rewards use existing owner contracts and must be proportionate to the actual work.

### Field 06 expansion — plan fit without duplicating sealed systems

The review packet names the current system responsible for each transition: request intake, site query, map access, construction action, material availability, labor assignment, communication, journal, and save. This list is not a list of new systems. At implementation time, record exact source evidence for each. If an owner already exposes a work order or construction project contract, extend it. If only the narrative layer is needed, use its established content path. If a new authority is required, stop and request a foreman decision with the smallest concrete contract proposal.

Check the live integration ledger, ownership claims, and current accepted debt before touching any related route, construction, trade, education, health, shelter, or accessibility package. A plan title is never sufficient evidence that a seam is still open. Search for producer, consumer, and save registration; test names may help locate code, but they do not prove wiring. Preserve no-op or incomplete content as a draft rather than adding a new local cache.

### Field 07 expansion — work order board and neighborhood notice states

The work board surfaces proposed, scheduled, active, waiting, inspection, maintenance, and closed work only where the current owner can support that distinction. A single project cannot appear as active and closed at the same time because of stale panel state. Filters should be optional and keyboard/controller accessible. A project list row shows location, requester, current status, last owner receipt, next action, and whether the public notice matches the latest update.

The project detail view separates public scope from internal authoring notes. Residents should not see invented budgets or hidden moral scores. If the current inventory can quote materials but not reserve them, the UI labels the quote as provisional. If a schedule is only proposed, do not present a countdown. If the work owner cannot confirm location, show the reported area as approximate.

Notices have a version, audience, source, and effective status. Replacing a notice requires a visible preview and, where appropriate, a confirmation. Closing the screen returns focus to the selected project row. Owner updates refresh content without stealing focus or resetting scroll position. A detail panel that cannot load a project should explain the missing reference and avoid a blank card.

### Field 08 expansion — fair process and conflict-aware language

Public works make disagreement visible but should not treat conflict as a minigame score. Dialogue distinguishes evidence from accusation. A resident can be mistaken without being malicious. A work crew can refuse a scope because it exceeds what can be supported. Public messaging names the affected site and action, not a character’s private history.

Candidate language:

- “The drain was inspected. The report does not establish where the blockage began.”
- “The repair is scheduled; materials have not been reserved.”
- “The entrance remains difficult to use. No access repair has been confirmed.”
- “The meeting moved to the lower hall. Two households asked to keep the original location.”
- “The tool is recorded at the workshop, but no return receipt is present.”
- “The notice is outdated according to the site owner’s latest receipt.”
- “This project is waiting for an inspection. No work has started.”
- “The handoff was recorded. Maintenance remains assigned to the current site owner.”

Accessibility review verifies that status is not color-only, action and cost are readable before commit, blocked interactions have a useful reason, and focus remains predictable. Conflict branches must remain understandable if the player does not visit every stakeholder. Avoid urgency copy when there is no real deadline.

### Field 09 expansion — concurrent projects and long-lived records

A future load profile should include several projects at mixed stages, two projects at one site, multiple notices with superseded revisions, and one work order whose latest observation contradicts its earlier inspection. Verify that opening a board does not repeatedly recompute every quote or rebuild all journal entries. Cache only derived presentation for the panel lifetime unless an existing owner provides its own cache. Keep save ownership with the system that controls the actual state.

Replay checks should use stable project IDs and deterministic choice sources. Randomized dialogue or notice ordering should not come from hash iteration order. A save after schedule acceptance must resume with the same commitment and must not reserve materials twice. A save after a work refusal must preserve the reason without presenting a completed task. A content removal test should confirm that closed historical records do not crash when a draft-only description is unavailable.

Measure project query time, number of visible rows, notice history growth, quote invalidations, and work-order detail refresh. Record baseline and build details before setting targets. UI virtualization is a candidate only if actual lists are large enough to warrant it; do not add a generic framework in anticipation of unmeasured scale.

### Field 10 expansion — first public works tranche and handoff evidence

Choose one site repair, one information correction, and one stakeholder disagreement for the first complete tranche. At least one project should end with an explicit unresolved item. Demonstrate the request, current-owner query, supported action, result receipt, public notice, journal history, and reopen or maintenance path. Include the exact catalog references and validation output in the eventual implementation handoff.

The acceptance dossier answers:

- Which source proves the reported defect exists?
- Which current owner controls the site and any route effect?
- Which system quotes or consumes materials?
- Which owner accepts labor and scheduling?
- How is inspection distinct from construction completion?
- Can the player see the exact remaining obligation?
- What remains true after save and resume?
- Can a revised notice preserve who saw the previous version?
- Does a resident objection remain visible after an alternate scope is chosen?
- Can the project be disabled without leaving a public notice that promises work?
- Is the playable result observable in the game rather than only in a plan or test?

No implementation begins until exact path ownership and current contract are recorded. A positive content review is not authorization to create a second construction or civic authority.


## Pass 12 — Work order lifecycle examples, public notice matrix, and maintenance return

This pass makes the public works plan easier to implement as content through existing owners. The work orders stay proposals until the current construction/site/inventory/duty owners can accept the described action. No new civic ledger or permanent project score is introduced.

### Field 01 expansion — a project has a public before and after

Before work, residents need to know what is being inspected, what will be disturbed, which access remains available, and when the next update is expected. During work, they need the difference between a confirmed schedule and a proposed time. After work, they need a scoped report: what changed, what could not be completed, who accepted the result, and who owns maintenance.

The project board uses an information path: request; source evidence; inspection; scope; public agreement; owner acceptance; work; verification; maintenance. Not every project reaches every stage. A request can be closed after inspection if there is no supported repair. A dispute can remain open while a separate urgent maintenance task proceeds, if the current owner allows it. The plan favors small, reviewable commitments instead of one broad “community improvement” score.

### Field 02 expansion — change control and receipt examples

When scope changes, preserve the original request and the reason for the revision. A new scope cannot silently replace a quote or accepted schedule. If an owner supports revisions, show what changed and request confirmation for a material change. If it does not, cancel through the owner and create a new work request.

Examples:

- Inspection found the handrail loose only at the upper post. Closeout says that specific post was repaired; it does not claim the full stair is new.
- The materials quote expired before work began. The project returns to planning; no stock was consumed.
- A resident withdrew a gate-access request. The record shows withdrawal by its source; related repair can remain active if it is separately justified.
- An alternate meeting space is proposed but has not been confirmed. The notice says “proposed” and retains the current location.
- A public work was completed, but the affected resident could not inspect it. The work result and acceptance status remain separate.
- A site owner reports that a path is usable but not wheelchair accessible. The record states that scope precisely rather than using a broad “open” label.

### Field 03 expansion — additional project packages

| Package | Inspection question | Public decision | Observable work result |
|---|---|---|---|
| West Stair Treads | Which treads are damaged, and what remains passable? | Close temporarily or keep a limited passage if the owner supports it | Site status and repair receipt |
| Common Wash Line | Does the shared line leak at one joint or several? | Schedule repair around current site use | Accepted maintenance result |
| Bell Tower Steps | Can a warning notice reach people who cannot climb the steps? | Add an alternate notice location | Notice audience and placement receipt |
| Clay Store Door | Is the doorway blocked by storage or a door fault? | Reorganize through inventory or request repair | Clear access only after owner confirmation |
| East Court Bench | Is the bench unsafe or merely uncomfortable? | Repair or remove from use through the site owner | Site use state and follow-up owner |
| Radio Room Shelf | Which equipment can be relocated without interrupting service? | Approve only the supported move window | Inventory and radio owner receipts |
| Shared Drying Rack | Several households need access at the same time | Set a public schedule or defer if no owner supports it | A visible, revisable schedule |
| North Lane Lamp | Is the lamp itself faulty or is its supply unavailable? | Inspect before promising repair | Current power/site result |
| Grain Store Threshold | Is the threshold damaged or obstructed by stored goods? | Separate construction scope from stock movement | Work and inventory outcomes |
| Lower Hall Eaves | Does the leak recur at the same location? | Authorize a bounded inspection | New observation linked to prior repair |
| Market Path Paint | Does the existing marking contradict the current route? | Replace outdated guidance | Current map or notice receipt |
| Workshop Waste Bin | Is the bin full, misplaced, or outside the current waste contract? | Request a collection or relocation if supported | Explicit owner acceptance or refusal |
| Water Point Queue Rail | Would a rail improve access or narrow the waiting path? | Consult both site users and owner | Accepted scope and dissent note |
| Library Crate Return | Which storage owner has the borrowed crates? | Agree a return route | Canonical item transfer |
| Shelter Privacy Screen | Do occupants request a screen and where may it be placed? | Ask for consent and site approval | Work only after both boundaries are accepted |
| Drying Room Vent | Is the vent blocked, broken, or simply closed? | Inspect before assigning maintenance | Owner-issued condition |
| Footbridge Marker | Is the marker missing or is the crossing status itself changed? | Correct signage only after route query | Marker record distinct from route state |
| Meeting Room Clock | Is the posted time unreliable or the event schedule stale? | Correct source of truth and announce it | Updated schedule with source |
| Tool Bench Light | Is task visibility affected by the light or another site condition? | Ask maintenance owner to inspect | Repair confirmation, not generic safety score |
| Quiet Lane Sign | Do neighbors want a notice or an enforceable restriction? | Publish only a supported public agreement | Notice receipt and review date |

Project variety should come from real differences in ownership and public effect. Rewording a repair as a quest does not make it a new project type.

### Field 04 expansion — maintenance stories after the ribbon is gone

**The handrail nobody owns.** A repair is finished, but residents disagree over who should inspect it next season. The player traces the site and work receipts, asks the current site owner to clarify responsibility, and publishes an accurate maintenance contact. The project closes only when the owner accepts the assignment; otherwise the unresolved responsibility is visible.

**The schedule that crowded the doorway.** A shared drying rack schedule was posted, but several residents were not consulted. The player can reopen the schedule, hear the missing group, and change it if the current event/site owner supports revision. The story shows that a nominally fair schedule can still exclude someone without making either group a villain.

**The borrowed fixtures.** A repair crew moved fixtures to clear a work area, but the inventory receipt is missing. The player checks the canonical item list, speaks to the custodian, and either records a transfer or leaves the location unknown. A side branch shows the crew setting a clearer handoff practice for future projects.

**The sign still points the wrong way.** A marker is fixed but the map owner has not confirmed the route. Residents want it left in place because the old route once helped them. The player can preserve the sign with an uncertainty note, request an owner check, or remove it if the actual owner command supports that action. The resolution remembers both the prior use and current evidence.

### Field 05 expansion — production checklist by project type

For access work, author an affected-user consultation, temporary access statement, inspection source, accepted work scope, and post-work check. For maintenance, author an observed fault, owner assignment, repair/refusal, and next inspection. For signage, author the source revision, audience, placement, effective status, and supersession history. For shared tools, author item identity, current custody evidence, transfer command, and return receipt. For scheduling, author participants, conflicts, confirmed window, announcement, and revision policy.

A task is not complete merely because the player visited a location. A maintenance visit can discover that no repair is needed, that the scope must be reduced, or that another owner should act. All are legitimate outcomes when the player can see why the task closes or stays open.

### Field 06 expansion — duplicate and decision-block audit

When project content intersects a completed plan, record how it reuses that plan’s owner rather than rebuilding it. If a path to a site exists, query the current map/travel route; do not add project-specific reachability. If a resident agreement touches relationships, use the current relationship owner’s supported fact; do not create a project approval meter. If a public notice uses radio or journal, reuse its current catalog and dispatch route. If a project requests a save field, identify the existing owning save section first.

Decision-blocked architecture remains blocked. A scenario writer cannot authorize a new material currency, work queue, durable labor schedule, or accessibility schema. The plan may propose those as explicit decisions with motivating evidence, but it cannot produce a mock implementation through a panel or JSON field.

### Field 07 expansion — notice audience and revision matrix

| Notice type | Minimum audience | Required review | Expiry or revision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temporary route closure | People using the affected route | Current route/site owner | Recheck when owner status changes |
| Proposed work schedule | Site users and affected crews | Work owner and current site owner | Expires when not accepted |
| Confirmed maintenance window | Affected occupants | Duty/site owner | Replaced by completion or cancellation receipt |
| Inspection result | Requester and authorized public audience | Inspection source | Superseded only by a newer result |
| Access alternative | People excluded by the original site | Site owner and affected users | Review after actual use |
| Tool custody change | Custodians and relevant crew | Inventory owner | Current until return or transfer |
| Meeting relocation | Invitees and current site users | Event/site owner | Ends after event or another revision |
| Unresolved issue | Requester and the agreed audience | Current owner if needed | Remains open until owner update |

The notice view allows a player to inspect its source and history. A proposed notice cannot be mistaken for a confirmed public instruction. Audience and privacy behavior must be resolved through existing communication contracts.

### Field 08 expansion — feedback for disputed work

Use language that reports the action and preserves disagreement:

- “The inspection confirmed damage at the upper post only.”
- “Work is scheduled, but no material has been reserved.”
- “The meeting move is proposed. The hall has not confirmed availability.”
- “The path is open according to the route owner; access limitations remain.”
- “The request was withdrawn. The separate maintenance issue remains open.”
- “The sign is corrected. The map owner has not verified the path.”
- “The work was completed. The resident review is still pending.”
- “No repair was accepted. The owner asked for a second inspection.”

The UX review checks that a player can see affected parties before agreeing, distinguish work scope from public impact, find the earlier notice, and revisit a project without losing scroll position. There is no moral score for resolving disagreement quickly.

### Field 09 expansion — project portfolio lifecycle pressure

A portfolio stress profile includes two projects at one site, a new request arriving during active work, one material quote expiring, a resident changing their request, an inspection that contradicts an earlier result, and a save after the public notice is proposed but before publication. The expected result is that one update does not overwrite a different project’s history and that failed actions do not reserve or consume resources.

Measure portfolio refresh cost at several active-project counts only after a current owner can supply them. Ensure that notices and receipts are indexed rather than reloaded from the full campaign history each frame. A small portfolio may not need virtualization. Avoid premature generic work-order frameworks; extend one current owner with the narrowest accepted contract.

### Field 10 expansion — public works commissioning package

The commissioning package includes one bounded maintenance repair, one corrected notice, and one project that closes with an unresolved objection. The tester or reviewer can trace the initiating report, owner command, actual work result, public statement, and save/resume behavior. It includes a screen flow, data examples in the current schema if approved, accessibility review, and evidence that disabled draft content creates no false public promise.

A project passes only if its result is observable in-game, durable where required, and consistent with the owner’s exact claim. The handoff records unimplemented maintenance or governance responsibilities rather than hiding them under “future polish.” No project count, word count, or number of authored notices substitutes for a truthful state transition.


## Pass 13 — Civic cast, public record fragments, and stewardship quests

This pass adds a story layer for long-lived public projects. The stories create civic texture, but every construction, custody, notice, schedule, and maintenance outcome still belongs to an existing owner.

### Field 01 expansion — a neighborhood is more than a project requester

Recurring characters represent different responsibilities: a repair lead who needs a precise work boundary, a host who worries about losing a meeting place, a records keeper who tracks old notices, a resident who uses the public route daily, a new apprentice who is learning the inventory handoff, and a mediator who can convene but cannot force agreement. A character can support one project and oppose another. Do not encode these changing views as a single goodwill score.

A public location accumulates history through dated repairs, names on notices, changed uses, and promises that were not fulfilled. Use those details as callbacks only when a current record supports them. The prose can acknowledge that residents remember a previous repair even if the exact owner record is unavailable, but it must not claim the repair changed current functionality.

### Field 02 expansion — civic quest contract

A civic quest distinguishes request, consultation, authorization, work, inspection, and follow-up. A conversation can produce an objection or a preference; it does not automatically approve construction. A completed work order can still lack resident review. A schedule can be confirmed by one owner and remain subject to another site constraint. The player-facing quest ledger displays the present boundary and next valid action.

Quest branches include agreement, partial agreement, rejection, withdrawal, delay, and missing authority. Every branch ends in a useful state: a documented choice, an unresolved responsibility, or a supported next task. “Choose a dialogue option and nothing happens” is not a complete branch.

### Field 03 expansion — additional stewardship quests

| Quest | Civic question | Player action | Durable callback |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Bench Beside the Door | Does the bench block the doorway or provide needed rest? | Ask users and inspect through the site owner | Later users describe actual access |
| A Notice for Night Shift | How do night workers receive a work closure update? | Select a supported channel and audience | A worker confirms or misses the notice |
| The Last Crate | Who owns a crate moved during repair? | Check canonical item custody | The next work crew signs the handoff |
| Names on the Wall | Should contributors be listed publicly? | Ask contributors and preview audience | A later resident opts in or out |
| The Room After Work | Can the gathering room reopen after maintenance? | Request a site-owner inspection | Status reflects the actual inspection |
| Path of Least Surprise | Which sign should a visitor follow? | Compare current route data with physical notice | The next traveler reports the source they used |
| A Place at the Table | A group asks for a meeting time other crews also need | Negotiate only through supported schedule owners | Affected groups receive the confirmed time |
| The Second Inspection | A repair receipt and a resident report differ | Reopen an inspection if current owner permits | Both observations remain visible |
| Storage for the Tools | A work crew needs a place to keep shared tools | Query current storage capacity and custody rules | Accepted storage or unresolved request |
| After the Delay | A project missed its proposed schedule | Publish the owner’s reason and next review | The affected group sees the new proposal |
| The Old Marker | A familiar sign points to an uncertain route | Preserve its history and request a current check | Replacement decision cites the map result |
| A Quiet Worksite | Neighbors request fewer disruptions | Ask the work owner what schedule can change | A revised notice or clear refusal |

### Field 04 expansion — four civic story beats

**The doorway and the bench.** The bench helps an older resident rest but narrows the entrance during crowded gatherings. The player can ask both users to describe the problem, request a site inspection, move the bench through an approved interaction, or leave it while posting a clear access note. The ending records who could use the doorway at the time; it does not call one group selfish.

**A message after the shift.** Night workers learn about maintenance after their shift has ended. A clerk proposes a notice at the common board, while the workers request a message they can read on return. The player checks which communication path exists, chooses the supported audience, and sees a later receipt if delivered. The clerk’s role changes from gatekeeper to editor of a shorter notice if the channel requires concise copy.

**The names on the wall.** A public repair plaque is proposed. One contributor wants recognition, one prefers not to be named, and a third objects to assigning credit to a single crew. The player can keep the wall informational without names, list consenting contributors through an approved interaction, or defer. The quest’s resolution focuses on truthful attribution rather than a prestige reward.

**The room after work.** A maintenance receipt states that work is complete, but the group organizer has not received confirmation that the room can reopen. The player queries the site owner and communicates only the returned status. The room may reopen, stay closed pending inspection, or be available with stated limits. No dialogue can override the site state.

### Field 05 expansion — observation and public notice fragments

Possible diegetic artifacts include a worksite clipboard with a dated scope, a notice board showing a superseded closure, a tool sign-out strip with a blank return, a resident letter asking for a quieter hour, a meeting agenda with two crossed-out rooms, an apprentice’s revised parts list, a hand-painted route sign, and an inspection note that distinguishes “dry today” from “leak repaired.” Each fragment should be short, attributable, and actionable or explicitly archival.

Side quests can ask the player to compare two fragments, find the person who authored one, obtain permission before publication, or preserve an unresolved disagreement. Avoid collecting documents merely to increase a lore count.

### Field 06 expansion — civic authority checklist

For each quest, identify who may request, who may approve, who may perform, who may inspect, who may publish a notice, and who may own future maintenance. One person may hold several roles, but the data should show the actual relationship. The UI cannot let the requester approve their own work unless the current contract allows it. If there is no approval authority, a character’s enthusiasm cannot create it.

Where a request overlaps an existing plan, the current plan owner receives the quest card and source references. Where an accepted owner exists, the story is an input to that owner. Where a proposed rule conflicts with a decision-blocked package, it stays as a question rather than bypassing the hold.

### Field 07 expansion — public history and private consultation

The public project summary shows request, scope, schedule, result, and unresolved obligations. Private consultation notes do not appear in the public history by default. If an objection is intended to be public, ask its author or use the established community record policy. The player can see when a notice changed and what receipt caused the revision.

The project panel offers separate views for work detail, public notice, and inspection history. It preserves selected tab and list position when refreshed. A notice with no current audience or owner receipt remains visibly a draft.

### Field 08 expansion — disagreement and consent copy

Sample lines for the player:

- “This inspection supports a repair at the upper post. The lower steps were not checked.”
- “The proposed schedule has not been accepted.”
- “Two groups requested different hours; no agreement is recorded.”
- “The room remains closed until the site owner confirms access.”
- “The contributor asked not to be named on the public notice.”
- “The tool is listed at the workshop, but no crew signed for its return.”
- “The closure notice was delivered to the day shift. Night shift receipt is still unknown.”
- “The repair was completed. Residents have not reviewed the result.”

A fair-process review ensures that “unresolved” is a legitimate state, dissent is not hidden behind a majority count, and the player sees when an action affects public access.

### Field 09 expansion — project history and future stewardship

Every completed project should point to the next responsible owner or say explicitly that no maintenance owner has accepted. A future inspection links back to the prior scope and result. If the site owner changes, old receipts remain attributable to the owner that issued them. Project history can be summarized for the current screen, but archival source records must not be rewritten.

### Field 10 expansion — quest acceptance and commissioning

A stewardship quest is accepted only when its initiating source, player command, result owner, closure state, public/private text, and optional sequel are specified. Reviewers check the accepted path plus at least one decline or dispute path. If a branch creates a new public record, its storage and audience must be supported. The quest can be published as narrative-only content only when it clearly avoids promising an operational change.


## Pass 14 — Worked project lifecycle and resident-facing proof

This walk-through ties one public repair to request intake, inspection, schedule, materials, labor, notices, and return. It does not claim these owners are currently connected; it defines the evidence a future accepted package must show.

### Field 01 expansion — opening request

Residents at North Lane report water collecting beside a shared path. One resident says the drain is blocked; another says the path dips below the drain and has always held water after rain. The request card names both sources separately. The board does not choose a culprit or assume a broken drain.

The player sees three next actions: request an inspection, publish a temporary caution if the site owner supports it, or leave the request pending. A detail view explains that inspection can identify the observed condition but may not determine its origin. The player requests inspection. The current site/maintenance owner returns a visit time or a refusal. If it has no inspection command, the project remains a content draft at this exact point.

### Field 02 expansion — scope and scheduling

The inspection records a shallow obstruction at one grate and no evidence about the lower path slope. The work packet scope is limited to clearing that grate. A separate note preserves the resident’s report about the path. The player queries the current inventory and duty owners for quote/availability. A quote is not a reservation. The schedule remains proposed until the construction or work owner accepts it.

Residents ask whether the path will be closed. The player checks the site owner’s access status. If no closure state is available, the notice says only that work is proposed and recommends caution without falsely claiming an official closure. If the owner confirms a limited closure, the notice identifies the affected segment and effective time.

### Field 03 expansion — public decision and notice

One resident wants work the next day; the crew says it can only attend later. A second household asks for a morning notice because they use the path before work. The player can accept the supported schedule, ask for a different window if supported, or defer the project. The UI displays which choice is confirmed and who has not responded.

The player publishes a notice through the current communication route. A sent receipt lists the audience; a queued receipt remains pending. The project detail stores a link to that receipt. The player cannot declare the whole lane closed from a local task card.

### Field 04 expansion — work and inspection

On the accepted work date, the work owner reports whether labor began and whether the scope changed. If material availability changed, the project returns to planning or continues only under the current contract. The player cannot force completion by advancing a scene.

The owner confirms that the grate was cleared. The player requests an inspection. The inspection confirms flow at that grate, while the lower path report remains unchecked. The closeout says exactly that. The project moves into maintenance follow-up only if an owner accepts responsibility. Otherwise, the player sees “No recurring inspection is assigned.”

### Field 05 expansion — character outcomes

The first resident accepts the narrow fix and asks that the lane be checked after the next rain. The second resident says the path slope remains their concern. The crew lead is glad that the task had a bounded scope and does not claim to have repaired more than it did. A clerk updates the notice with the new result. The player’s journal shows the two residents’ different positions and the owner’s confirmed work outcome.

An optional quest asks the player to bring the unresolved slope report to the correct site owner. If the site owner accepts it, a separate inspection can be scheduled. If it refuses, the quest closes as “report received; inspection unavailable,” keeping the concern visible without creating a fake future project.

### Field 06 expansion — integration trace and failure probes

A reviewer follows request creation to the site owner, inspection source to work quote, quote to accepted schedule, work action to completion receipt, inspection to closeout, notice to communication receipt, and save/load to persistent history. At each stage, the reviewer verifies that the same owner controls the state shown in the panel.

Failure probes include: no inspection route, no duty crew, unavailable material, declined notice delivery, schedule conflict, changed scope, and save before work starts. The player sees what failed and whether any work or resource was committed. A panel error must not mutate project status.

### Field 07 expansion — example board state progression

- Request received: “Two reports; cause not confirmed.”
- Inspection scheduled: “One grate will be inspected; path slope excluded.”
- Quote shown: “Estimate returned; materials not reserved.”
- Schedule accepted: “Work window confirmed for the next available crew.”
- Notice pending: “The channel has queued the update.”
- Work started: “The work owner reports the grate task in progress.”
- Work completed: “The grate was cleared; the lower path was not inspected.”
- Inspection closed: “Flow was confirmed at the grate.”
- Maintenance handoff: “No recurring inspection is assigned.”
- Project history: “The slope concern remains open as a separate request.”

The board shows only the current summary by default and retains each prior receipt in history.

### Field 08 expansion — response and disagreement language

The project text uses: “The inspection found an obstruction at the grate.” It does not say “The residents were right about the whole lane.” The closeout says: “Flow was confirmed at the grate. The path slope was not part of this work.” If a crew refuses the schedule, the notice says: “No work date is confirmed.” If a household does not receive the notice, the UI does not claim that every resident was informed.

The player is allowed to complete the bounded repair while leaving a separate complaint open. This prevents the narrative from forcing one consensus outcome and keeps the actual work receipt useful.

### Field 09 expansion — persistence and workload checks

Save after request intake, inspection, quote, accepted schedule, queued notice, work start, completion, and inspection. Reload each boundary and check that no resource is consumed twice, a queued notice is not duplicated, and the unresolved path concern remains visible. Open this project alongside several unrelated work orders to verify that its refresh does not rewrite other histories.

Measure the number of owner calls for list rendering and detail opening. A board render should not issue a new materials quote every frame. Quotes are refreshed at explicit points or on supported invalidation events. Project history can summarize receipts but does not replace them.

### Field 10 expansion — commissioning decision

The worked project qualifies as a playable prototype only if each step returns a real owner receipt and the stated boundary is preserved. If the work owner can clear the grate but has no inspection receipt, the release wording must not say “verified.” If the notice route cannot report delivery, the UI must say “drafted” or “queued” as appropriate. If no maintenance owner accepts follow-up, the project remains closed with that obligation explicitly unassigned.

The integration handoff documents exact owner paths, data references, UI state, save contract, denial results, performance observation, and which related site condition remains untouched. This project is a model for the public works content pack, not evidence that all listed project types are implemented.


## Pass 15 — Recurring maintenance calendar, work portfolio, and stewardship handoffs

This pass adds depth after construction: recurring inspection, responsible ownership, public history, and project closure. It does not create a new maintenance scheduler. Recurrence exists only where an existing owner can schedule it.

### Field 01 expansion — durable works require a named next step

A public work changes the built environment only through its current owner. The community plan adds the question of what happens after the work: who checks it, how a resident reports a new problem, and how a later crew finds the accepted scope. A project without maintenance ownership remains useful if its closeout says “no recurring owner accepted.” It must not display a fake repeating task.

For recurring work supported by an existing schedule owner, the player can see the next due step, last result, and deferral reason. For one-time work, the board shows a completed scope and a route for a new request. Completion does not guarantee permanence. New damage or a contradictory observation opens a new report only through existing event or request seams.

### Field 02 expansion — maintenance handoff record

The candidate handoff identifies completed work, inspected area, excluded area, named current owner, next inspection only if scheduled, public notice, accepted resident review, and unresolved concern. If responsibility moves between owners, the transfer is explicit. A new owner’s refusal leaves responsibility unassigned and calls for escalation through current governance.

A handoff never rewrites the construction receipt. The original contractor’s statement, inspector’s result, and resident review remain separate sources. If the sources disagree, the panel displays the difference and offers a supported query or new inspection. It cannot pick the “best” source by recency alone unless the owner’s contract says that is authoritative.

### Field 03 expansion — recurring service candidates

| Service family | Inspection trigger | Example return result | Owner boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shared path | New report or existing schedule | Clear, restricted, or unverified | Current route/site owner |
| Public stairs | New inspection request | One section checked; remainder excluded | Site or construction owner |
| Notice board | Content revision or public report | Current, stale, or unreadable | Notice/content owner |
| Shared tool store | Missing/returned custody receipt | Located, transferred, or unknown | Inventory owner |
| Meeting room | Before a scheduled use | Available, limited, or closed | Site/event owner |
| Water-point queue area | New access request | Site observation and accepted scope | Water/site owner |
| Repair bench | Work order or damage observation | Usable or awaiting repair | Maintenance owner |
| Storage room | Inventory or access report | Capacity result from owner | Storage owner |
| Public lamp | Owner-emitted fault or inspection | Operational status or no result | Power/site owner |
| Work schedule | Accepted assignment or change | Confirmed or pending | Duty/work owner |
| Crossing sign | Map or site revision | Matches, conflicts, or uncertain | Map/notice owner |
| Shelter screen | Occupant request and site approval | Accepted placement or declined | Site and privacy owner |

These are candidate content categories, not a list of missing features. Each category is cut if its owner does not expose a source and result.

### Field 04 expansion — stewardship mini-campaign

**First season: identify the owner.** The player encounters several small failures and learns that each belongs to a different owner. A notice board is outdated, a tool is missing, and a room needs inspection. The campaign asks the player to route each request correctly rather than solve all three directly.

**Second season: close the loop.** A prior work receipt is challenged by new evidence. The player must decide whether to reopen inspection, publish a correction, or record an unresolved finding. An apprentice helps link old and new reports.

**Third season: hand responsibility onward.** A crew is leaving its post. The player chooses what must be handed off, what is still pending, and what cannot be promised. If an owner accepts the assignment, the game records the transfer. If not, the ending identifies the unassigned obligation and the person who raised it.

This arc makes maintenance and institutional memory playable without inventing a background decay model.

### Field 05 expansion — stewardship and continuity quests

- Review a prior work scope before requesting more work.
- Find the owner of an unassigned maintenance obligation.
- Ask a resident to inspect only the area within their knowledge.
- Publish a corrected schedule after owner confirmation.
- Return tools and link the transfer to the project.
- Reopen a closed request after a new source arrives.
- Mark one section checked and another explicitly excluded.
- Invite a new crew member to review the accepted work receipt.
- Close a recurring task through the current scheduler, if available.
- Explain that a recurring inspection is not scheduled.
- Compare repair and resident observations without discarding either.
- Carry a maintenance handoff to the next duty owner.
- Ask a project requester whether the original concern persists.
- Update a public contact only when the owner supports the change.
- Keep an unresolved item visible in the project board.

### Field 06 expansion — durable integration, save, and migration

Stateful work history uses the existing project/site/journal owner. A separate public works save section is forbidden unless the current architecture explicitly assigns one. Before integration, map capture and restore for every stateful receipt. Confirm deterministic order for event application and save checksums. If a catalog ID changes, update references through its owning migration path and retain active project history.

Content migration must handle a removed notice or retired quest. The saved owner receipt should remain readable even if the current description is no longer offered. A fallback summary is preferable to silently dropping a historical project.

### Field 07 expansion — public portfolio lifecycle view

The portfolio distinguishes active work, scheduled work, completed scope, maintenance due, and unresolved responsibility only if the current owners can produce each status. A “maintenance due” badge is not computed from panel time. Users can filter by location and requester, but public/private visibility follows current record policies. Closing a project takes the player back to its predecessor or the same list position.

### Field 08 expansion — future promises and honest language

- “This site owner has accepted the next inspection.”
- “No recurring inspection was scheduled.”
- “The work receipt covers the upper landing only.”
- “The resident report is newer, but it has not been inspected.”
- “The project is complete within its stated scope.”
- “Responsibility for future maintenance remains unassigned.”
- “The request is reopened because new evidence arrived.”
- “The work order is still active; no completion receipt exists.”

These lines let the player distinguish completed work from future reliability. The game should not promise “maintained” when it only knows “repaired once.”

### Field 09 expansion — project archive maintenance

An archive needs a stable key, owner, and bounded summary query. When old projects age, keep source receipts accessible without loading every detail into the active board. Search results show why a project matched. The archive can group related projects by site, but that grouping remains derived presentation rather than a new authority.

### Field 10 expansion — stewardship release evidence

A completed public works tranche demonstrates at least one one-time repair, one revised notice, one unassigned maintenance case, and one later return based on new evidence. It proves that the game can close a narrow scope without implying broad service guarantees. The review records which history owner retains the event, how the UI surfaces it, how removal/migration behaves, and where a new report begins.


## Pass 16 — Work order acceptance examples

This closing tranche is a quick review deck for project authors and integrators. Its cases test scope, notice, and lifecycle boundaries.

### Fields 01–03 — project status cases

| Project moment | Truthful status | Claim that needs separate evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Resident reports a leak | Request received | Cause or extent of the leak |
| Inspector visits one corner | Partial inspection | Whole-site safety |
| Material quote returned | Estimate available | Stock reserved |
| Crew accepts a date | Work scheduled | Work started |
| Crew reports completion | Work completed within stated scope | Inspection accepted |
| Notice is queued | Update pending relay | Audience received it |
| Resident disagrees with result | Review requested or disagreement recorded | Repair failed |
| New report arrives later | New evidence received | Old receipt invalid |

A reviewer can identify the source and owner for every status. If the status has no owner, it remains narrative text and cannot drive project lifecycle.

### Fields 04–07 — project branch sample

For the North Lane drain, the supported outcomes are: inspection finds a bounded obstruction; inspection finds no obstruction; access is unavailable; owner declines the proposed scope; or the resident withdraws the request. Each has a clear task result. A separate lower-path concern can remain open. The public notice follows only the accepted work and confirmed site status.

Work, inspection, and resident review are separate rows in the history. A revised scope requires a new quote or explicit owner revision. The UI retains the previous scope and explains which fact changed.

### Fields 08–10 — closure and durability review

Reviewers save after request, quote, schedule, notice, work start, completion, and inspection. They confirm there are no double transfers, duplicate notices, missing dissent records, or unowned maintenance claims. They also test a project whose description has been removed from new content while its saved receipt remains available.

The project counts as playable only if the owner’s work result appears in-game, the public notice matches that result, and the project can close within scope without claiming broader service. A narrative-only proposal is kept outside playable totals. The handoff lists every unresolved owner decision plainly.


## Pass 17 — One public works packet, fully annotated

A candidate project called “North Lane Drain, bounded inspection” shows how the request, scope, and notice align. The working key is provisional. Two residents provide reports, one describing standing water and the other noting that the path dips. Neither report proves a drain defect. The project begins with an inspection request, not a repair promise.

The work packet identifies the location, both sources, inspected boundary, excluded lower path, current site owner, inspection command, and expected result. It queries duty and inventory owners only after the inspection supports a bounded scope. A returned quote is labeled as an estimate. A schedule remains proposed until the construction/work owner accepts it. The temporary public notice names the affected grate and does not close the whole lane unless the site owner supplies that state.

If the work owner accepts and completes clearing the grate, its receipt records that exact scope. A separate inspection confirms or refuses the result. The lower path concern remains open. A resident can accept the bounded repair and still request another visit. Another resident can disagree with the scope without blocking unrelated maintenance. The project’s ending says what was done, what was not checked, and who owns the next action if any.

The UI has a portfolio row, project detail, scope preview, notice preview, and history. It differentiates request, inspection, estimate, schedule, work start, completion, and inspection. A queued notice is not shown as delivered. The public view omits private consultation details. Keyboard/controller navigation preserves focus and returns the player to the selected row after closing the source note.

Save boundaries include request intake, inspection, quote, schedule acceptance, notice dispatch, work completion, and final inspection. Reload must not double-transfer materials, duplicate notices, or erase either resident’s report. Performance review observes project list refresh, detail queries, and notice history with several other active works. No recurring inspection is shown unless the current scheduler accepts it.

The handoff lists current source and owner paths, data schema/validator, construction and inventory contracts, save owner, player action, actual receipt, unsupported branches, and the distinction between completed scope and future maintenance. The example is rejected if the panel declares the lane safe, consumes inventory from an estimate, closes the lower path concern, or creates a local project-complete flag that disagrees with the work owner.


A public project should be readable by someone who did not initiate it. The board therefore links every status to a source note and explains technical terms in plain language. An accepted scope includes its exclusions in the public summary when those exclusions affect access or safety. A closed scope can be reopened only through a new report or an owner-supported correction; editing old prose cannot change the project’s real state. If a resident submits a new observation after closure, preserve the original closeout and attach the new report. A reviewer checks that the player can discover this route without navigating a hidden debug or administrator surface. These small affordances make civic work a playable long-term system rather than a list of one-off construction rewards.

When two projects share one site, each keeps its own scope and owner receipts while the presentation may show their relationship. A drain repair and a meeting relocation can affect the same lane, but completing the meeting task cannot close the drain request. If one project blocks another, the responsible owner returns the dependency and the board explains it. Authors should include at least one test case where a new public request arrives during active work; the player can inspect it without silently changing the accepted scope. Project links are references, not shared mutable completion state. This prevents a broad site-level “fixed” flag from erasing a narrower unfinished obligation.

## Pass 18 — Construction-owner collision map and public-service expansion boundary

This pass revises the public works proposal against current implementation evidence. It distinguishes a public works content loop from the already integrated construction, colony, map, and weather authorities.

### Field 01 expansion — build and renovation already have owners

ShelterExpansionSystem already owns shelter room construction, renovation, upgrades, stability, and project state through shelter_construction.json. ColonySystem owns outpost/colony structures and blueprints, including the field-clinic post. The live integration ledger records Plan 156 for physical shelter expansion and Plan 160 for expedition colony/outpost construction. Plan 135 owns cross-system weather effects, Plan 163 owns cartography, Plan 162 owns archive history, and inventory remains canonical.

Therefore this plan is not a new construction engine or another materials/labor ledger. Its potential value is the player-facing public request, consultation, scope communication, and route between existing projects and people. Any work action that cannot be represented through a current owner stays a design question. Do not add a generic works queue as a way to make content cards clickable.

### Field 02 expansion — recognize the difference between a service request and a build
